A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same DSGD convergence work, with readable text, equations, proofs, and appendices. The added material can be distinguished from retained content, including v1 Appendix G, which becomes v2 Appendix K.

before.justification: V1 reports theoretical results and proofs. Its main text and Appendices A–G contain no original experimental, simulation, or data-analysis outcomes.

after.justification: V2 Appendix G reports original simulations of decentralized quadratic optimization, with MSE and empirical tail-probability results in Figures 1–2.

M1.justification: Algorithm 1 retains the same adapt-then-combine update. However, Theorem 1 and Appendix E revise the prescribed non-convex fixed step size by changing its denominator from a factor sqrt(dT) to sqrt(dLT), a limited learning-rate revision.

E1.justification: V1 has no empirical evaluation coverage. V2 adds evaluations on synthetic 50-dimensional strongly convex quadratic objectives with heterogeneous local costs, Gaussian gradient noise, and static Erdős–Rényi communication networks.

E2.justification: Neither version empirically evaluates competing algorithms against DSGD. V2 Figures 1–2 compare DSGD across network sizes and thresholds; the comparisons with other algorithms remain theoretical.

E3.justification: Appendix G introduces complete evaluation protocols: zero initialization, step size 1/(t+1), 10,000 iterations for 30 users, and 3,000 iterations for 25, 50, and 100 users. The scaling experiment controls connectivity near lambda=0.6 and heterogeneity. Metrics include average squared distance to the optimum and tail probabilities at three accuracy thresholds.

E4.justification: V2 adds a controlled network-size sensitivity study testing the predicted speed-up while keeping connectivity and heterogeneity comparable. It also examines tail decay at thresholds 10^-2, 10^-3, and 10^-4 and relates delayed decay to MSE behavior. V1 contains no corresponding empirical analyses.

E5.justification: V2 introduces repeated-run and Monte Carlo estimation procedures: 5,000 runs with 3,000 sampled run indices per iteration for Figure 1, and 1,000 runs with 600 sampled indices for Figure 2. V1 has no empirical statistical reporting. The new MSE plots contain shaded bands whose statistical meaning is unspecified.

E6.justification: Figures 1–2 add the first empirical convergence and tail-probability curves. They show faster observed decay with increasing network size. At threshold 10^-4, the 25-user tail probability remains one within the allotted iterations, while the 50-user curve only begins declining. These are newly reported results, without earlier empirical values for comparison.

T1.justification: V2 revises Theorem 1's step-size prescription and parameter dependence, including correcting its stated network term to use the squared spectral gap appearing in the proof. Appendix F revises the assembled strongly convex bound to retain explicit initialization and parameter factors. New Appendices H–J add transient-time derivations, mathematical arguments about linear speed-up, and assumption A1' with a transition-matrix argument for time-varying networks.

C1.justification: The abstract and principal contributions retain optimal HP convergence, relaxed gradient assumptions, and linear speed-up. The conclusion additionally claims transient times matching or improving upon corresponding MSE-based bounds, extending one aspect of the paper's claimed contribution.

C2.justification: V2 substantially expands interpretations of network, noise, and heterogeneity effects and explains the significance of transient times. Appendix I develops why uniform MGF bounds can conceal constants that cancel speed-up, while Appendix J discusses applicability to time-varying directed networks. The existing dimension-dependence limitations remain in Appendix K.

D1.justification: Appendix G adds implementation information absent from v1: scikit-learn's make_sparse_spd_matrix with dimension 50 and alpha=0.9, specified local linear-term distributions, Metropolis–Hastings communication weights, a Gaussian gradient oracle, and initialization and step-size details. These provide a concrete recipe for the new simulations.

R1.justification: V2 adds Alghunaim and Yuan [68] as a transient-time comparison and substantially expands positioning against Lu et al. [57] and centralized HP analyses. Sections 3.2–3.3 and Appendices H–J compare network assumptions, step-size choices, variance reduction, and transient bounds. Additional weighting and graph references support the new material.

P1.justification: The main section order and most existing exposition remain. Post-theorem discussions are reorganized into labeled topics, wording and cross-references are refined, and the appendix roadmap is expanded. The former dimension-dependence Appendix G is relabeled K.

P2.justification: V2 introduces two substantive experimental figures: Figure 1 has two panels, and Figure 2 has four. They add logarithmic performance plots, legends, shaded MSE bands, and explanatory captions. V1 has no corresponding figures; the existing single-column format and algorithm display are retained.

improvement.justification: V2 aligns Theorem 1's stated network dependence with its derivation and adds documented, controlled simulations illustrating the retained convergence and scaling claims. The expanded discussion also makes the guarantees easier to interpret. These are useful but limited gains: the central results remain largely intact, and the empirical evidence covers only quadratic problems with undefined MSE shading.
